name: Corpse paint

lead: Corpse paint is a style of face makeup used by heavy metal and especially black metal musicians. The face and neck are made white or pale, while the areas around the eyes and mouth are blackened, sometimes with red marks suggesting wounds. The goal is a deliberately inhuman, corpse-like or demonic appearance rather than conventional attractiveness.

It matters to appearance as a transformative makeup look: it reshapes how contrast, hollows and facial structure read, and it is widely used as a costume, stage identity and subcultural marker. Historians trace it through 1960s and 1970s shock rock to the Norwegian black metal scene of the early 1990s.

paras: Practitioners apply a pale base across the face and neck, then use black around the eyes and mouth and often along the cheekbones, adding personal patterns. Many bands develop a signature design. It is applied with ordinary face paint or cream makeup and removed after the performance.

The risks are those of any heavy face paint: possible skin irritation or reactions to products, and the time needed to apply and remove it. Some bands associated with the style have also been linked to violent or controversial episodes in the wider scene, which coverage of the genre discusses separately.

angle.text: Corpse paint is makeup applied directly to the skin, so the change in appearance is immediate and lasts for as long as it is worn. It is used to adopt a deliberately macabre persona, and its strong contrast changes how facial structure and expression read on stage or in photographs.

lead: Corpse paint is a form of stage makeup associated with heavy metal, and above all with black metal. The face and neck are whitened, the eyes and mouth are ringed in black, and red marks suggesting blood or lacerations are sometimes added, producing a look intended to appear dead, inhuman or demonic.[1][2]

As a way of changing how a face looks, it works through strong contrast: dark sockets and mouth against pale skin exaggerate bone structure and hollows. Musicians use it to create a persona distinct from their everyday appearance, and individual players often settle on a signature design.[1]

Its lineage runs through 1960s shock rock, including Screamin' Jay Hawkins, Screaming Lord Sutch and Arthur Brown, and 1970s acts such as Alice Cooper and Kiss, before becoming a fixture of metal in the late 1970s and 1980s and of the Norwegian black metal scene in the early 1990s.[1] No clinical studies of the practice exist.

paras: The standard look whitens the face and neck and blackens the areas around the eyes and mouth. Red marks suggesting blood or lacerations are sometimes added, and other colours are uncommon, with exceptions such as Attila Csihar, Satyricon and Dodheimsgard.[1] Musicians commonly develop a recognisable personal pattern.[1]

Similar body and face painting appeared in 1960s rock, worn by Screamin' Jay Hawkins, Screaming Lord Sutch and Arthur Brown; Brown's 1968 performance of "Fire" is said to have inspired Alice Cooper, who wore black-and-white paint in the 1970s alongside acts such as Kiss and Lou Reed.[1] King Diamond is reported to have used corpse-like paint as early as 1978 with his band Black Rose.[1]

Per "Dead" Ohlin of Mayhem began wearing it in the late 1980s and was the first to link the paint explicitly to looking like a corpse; bandmate Necrobutcher credits him with the term and says Ohlin wanted to look dead rather than cool.[1] In the early 1990s other Norwegian bands followed and the style spread worldwide. The Brazilian band Sarcofago is also credited as a pioneer, a claim Necrobutcher disputes on Mayhem's behalf.[1]

The paint was intended to make performers look inhuman, corpse-like or demonic, and early on to emphasise their features while making them appear dead.[1] Some Norwegian bands, including Emperor and Satyricon, later stopped wearing it, citing a loss of individual meaning and its growing trendiness.[1] Professional wrestlers such as Sting and Vampiro adopted similar looks, and it is also used as general cosmetic ornamentation.[1]

timeline.event: Arthur Brown performs "Fire" in dramatic face paint, later cited as an influence on Alice Cooper.[1]
